I teach one habit and everything else follows from it. Before you agree or disagree with anything, find the sentence the whole thing rests on. It is almost never the conclusion.
And in this piece it is in a footnote, which is either careless or very deliberate.
Careless, I would say, and that is the more interesting case. He knows the field well enough to have stopped noticing that the definition is contested.
The four studies are the part I keep returning to. Four sources, none of which defines the term the same way.
And two of which were built to answer something else entirely. Which does not make them irrelevant — it makes them evidence for a question nobody in this article is asking.
So what would you say to him, if he were sitting here? Because I would not want to say the piece is worthless. It is not.
I would say: paragraph six is a leap, and you are entitled to make it, and you have to say that you are making it. That is the whole complaint.
Which is a smaller complaint than it sounds and a more serious one than it looks.

Before you decide whether you agree, do this. Find the sentence the argument rests on. It is almost never the conclusion, it is frequently in the middle, and in about one case in five it is in a footnote. Second thing, and this one surprises people. A strong opening is not evidence that the rest is strong. It is the opposite of a guarantee. A watertight first section earns trust, and trust is exactly what a weak third section spends. So read the beginning generously and the middle suspiciously. And here is my test for a leap. Two facts, both true, and the second presented as a consequence of the first. Ask two questions. Is a mechanism proposed by which one produces the other? And does the author say, in their own words, that they are making an inference? If the answer to both is no, you have found the place where the argument stops being an argument.

I want to defend him, up to a point, and I will start by giving away the strongest objection. Paragraph six does not follow. He should have written one sentence saying that he was inferring rather than reporting, and he did not, and that is a real fault. Now the defence. If we require a demonstrated mechanism for every inference in a piece of this length, nothing gets written at all, and the journals fill up with papers that establish nothing carefully. As for the four studies using four definitions, I would ask you to name me a field in which any two studies use identical definitions. There is no such field. Pointing that out is not a finding, it is a description of research, and a review that treats it as a discovery is doing something rather like what it accuses him of.
